extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and students of the craft of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using pictorial scene-making and dramatic method in fiction: how to prepare scenes, represent time, choose focalization/narration, and shape characters so action attains force without losing verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial impression as agent of drama
rubrics_metrics.description: “a pictorial impression, wrought to the right pitch, will speed the work of drama—will become an effective agent in the book, instead of remaining the mere decorative introduction that it may seem to be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a vivid, well-rendered scene before the action so that the picture itself supplies reserve force for the drama; the picture should do work in the book (supply atmosphere, stakes, and continuity), not merely decorate. Example: Balzac’s preparatory pictures make his action start forward with a reserve of vigour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background characters must shed irrelevant life
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who reappear from other books must, when incidental to the foreground action, 'shed their irrelevant life'; otherwise they 'disturb the unity of the story and confuse its truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only carry forward associations from other works when those associations are relevant to the present story. Bringing a character’s unrelated past into an incidental role creates distracting relations between that character and the reader that do not serve the foreground action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical interweaving of separate pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: The artificial design of interlocking books (recurrence of old names) is not an enhancement of an individual book's art and can be 'more mechanical than artistic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on clever cross-book entanglement to produce density of life in a single story; judge each story on its own unity and whether borrowed associations genuinely contribute to the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial setting to temper excessive drama
rubrics_metrics.description: When action 'is likely to seem harsh, overcharged, romantic, it is made to look less so, less hazardous and more real, by recourse to the art of the picture-maker.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the dramatic material risks seeming implausible or melodramatic, embed it in believable, richly observed surroundings to extenuate and authenticate it. Example: Balzac embedding romance or crime in a sober background to disguise falsity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile romance with realistic background
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a fantastic tale pass for reality, 'get the tale firmly embedded in a background of truth; its falsity may be disguised.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tonal and imagistic consistency between extraordinary plot elements and the realistic world you present; mismatch (gaudy romance vs sober fact) exposes falsity. Dickens is praised for merging both without sharp distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce violent drama gradually through prepared scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Dickens’s method: 'lead gradually into [romantic intrigues], through well-populated scenes of character and humour; so that his world is actual ... by the time that his plot begins to thicken.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before unleashing the climax or violent drama, immerse the reader in a broad, believable world populated with character and humour so the climax feels earned and credible (e.g., Bleak House).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer dramatic presentation (action/dialogue) to abstract summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Dickens 'is always readier to work in action and dialogue than to describe at large; he is happier in placing a character there before us, as the man or woman talked and behaved in a certain hour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for immediacy and vividness, show characters via scenes and dialogue rather than summarizing their lives at a distance. Exception: when a broad, pictured summary better serves the book's aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharp, concentrated characterization for minor figures
rubrics_metrics.description: When characters appear only briefly within a pictured action, 'they must be all of it within narrow bounds ... reduced to the expedient of labelling his people with a trick or a phrase.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For minor or scene-only characters, crystallize them with one or two striking traits, phrases, or habits so they function effectively in the limited space allotted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative standpoint as a tool to tone drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of first person can either 'work the drama into a picture' or shift a book toward pictured impression, depending on subject (examples: Esmond, The Master of Ballantrae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a narrator/focalization that modulates how the drama is perceived—first person may cushion raw action through subjective reflection or heighten immediacy; pick based on the emotional and tonal needs of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough, precise material scene-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac’s method: describe rooms, approach, furniture—'down to the vases on the mantelpiece or the pots and pans in the cupboard'—as 'an essential preliminary to the story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete, specific details of place when those details are integral to the story’s meaning or will be used in the action; present them confidently so the reader accepts the scene as complete and operative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail-listing works only if the author possesses the image
rubrics_metrics.description: A mechanical sum of details makes no image; Balzac succeeds because 'he, more than anyone else, knows everything' he describes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid exhaustive inventories unless the writer truly imagines the place; otherwise details will read hollow. Full description must be motivated by an internalized image, not by obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare time’s impression in the picture to allow temporal compression
rubrics_metrics.description: By preparing the life, routine and scene (e.g., Maison Grandet), Balzac can write 'Five years went by in this way' without loss—the sense of duration is latent in the picture already prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To compress long spans without exhaustive interior narration, establish environmental and habitual facts early so the reader intuitively senses the passage of time; then concise temporal statements can suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relieve climax by preparing everything beforehand
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax 'ought to complete, to add the touch that makes the book whole ... It should be free to do what it must without any unnecessary distraction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overburdening the climax with exposition or trying to accomplish too much at that point. Let the climax perform its concluding function by having background, character, and thematic groundwork already in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain iterative escalation when subject demands repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: For a subject that is a series of similar effects (e.g., La Recherche de l’Absolu), 'the book must remain throughout, reiterating one effect with growing intensity—always at the pitch of high hope and sharp disappointment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the narrative’s core is repetitive escalation, maintain strict control of pace and intensity so each recurrence deepens rather than bores; vary emphasis subtly to heighten stakes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose external or internal focus based on character depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a character 'lacks the poetry, the inner resonance' (e.g., Eugénie), it is 'much better to look at it from outside' than to try to render a prolonged interior monologue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to render a story from a character’s interior or from exterior presentation depending on whether that character can sustain prolonged psychological interest; external pictorial method can better carry stories of low-inward-resonance material.
